Several of them make deviations from the task law: merged previews (impl-F/test/history.test.mjs:196), commitPreview returning '' (impl-F/test/history.test.mjs:216-225), and spots being settable only by tools (impl-F/test/validation.test.mjs:59). cross.generativity: Yes, strongly. All six independently arrived at the same core. Crop and spot centres are stored as fractions of the frame and converted once in setCropFromView and addSpotFromView. Validation is one central applyMutation/setPath dispatch. Atomicity comes from applying to a clone. An append-only entries list sits beside a separate undo structure. A v1 document is converted to fractions on load. geometryAt multiplies and rounds at 1e-6 or 1e-9. The details differ in three places. Undo mechanism: inverse mutations (A, D), replay from a base (B, E, F) or before/after snapshots (C). Radius unit: a fraction of the width (A to D), of the shorter side (E), or original pixels with sqrt(sx*sy) (F). Migration seam: only A has a table and a runner; the rest use a hard-coded dispatch. The chapter's Compiler shrank everywhere to geometryAt, and its unit tags appear only in A, as strings.
cross.worse_is_better: Partly. B (600 lines) and E (642 lines) reach almost the same behavioural quality as A (945 lines) with replay-based undo: undo is a cursor move or a stack pop, and no inverses, MISSING sentinel, recordPathOf or diffStates are needed. For a document of a few fields, replay or snapshots (C) are simpler and correct, so the chapter's 'transactions that record their inverse' asks for more than this task needs. A's extra size does pay off in one place: its migrations table is the only design where change request 2 composes without rewriting the v1 migration. That part of the yardstick is worth its cost.
